title: Tin Roof Blues, the tenor in Chicago and clarinet parts
summary: Ashcraft describes Rapolo's chorus, George Johnson's influence on Eddie Miller, and how tenor changed ensemble voicing.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Yes. Strangely enough, the Tin Roof Blues was made by Rapolo. I'm saying Rapolo. It was actually the Rhythm Kings, of course. But Rapolo's chorus had that thing barred, not officially by anybody, but it wasn't allowed in some of the soda fountains. It was definitely thought to be too sexy or suggestive for anybody. I'd forgotten that. One effect that I'd kind of like to have a part of this, because I don't think anybody else has paid any attention to it, was the effect of the tenor in Chicago. You see, there was no tenor in New Orleans that I knew of.
Oh, well, not until quite a bit later when Eddie Miller became the nominee.

Oh, yes, but earlier. And as far as Chicago knew, I mean, Chicago originated it. I haven't talked to Eddie about it, but I think... I think so. I know that Eddie told me that... Eddie was quite familiar with Pettis, although I think he told me that the most important guy for him early was George Johnson on the Wolverines, a greatly underestimated guy, who I might add would have gone a great deal further. He was a great friend of Hoagie's and was probably more responsible for the rhythm in that band than anybody, including Vicks. If his father, who was desperately sick, hadn't made him promise to give up the horn. And the tragedy of it was that his father died, and after that George Johnson told me he got the first good offer to play the horn he'd ever had in his life. What I wanted to say about this was that when the clarinets, the parts they were playing in the New Orleans type of music, didn't allow for a tenor. You see, the clarinet was playing a second part, really. Like Timmy Noon. He played the E in a C chord, for instance, where the trumpet would be playing the C. Or the, let's say, he'd be playing the melody. And Brunus, or the trombone player, who was playing fundamentally the bass or third part. Well, when the tenor came in and started playing second, it moved the clarinets up to third. And you'll find that it made a third difference. It made the clarinets higher, actually. And the best example I can think of is Rosie McHarg, who plays a pure clarinet. It's very much like Larry Shields did, even though he didn't have a tenor in the band.
It wasn't a case of the tenor replacing the trombone. No, the tenor. Having a tonality.
Of course it was low. And trombone players hate a band with a tenor in it. Right? They still do.
They wondered whether the conflict might arise from the tenor seeking too often the trombone note.

A tenor, as they originally played it, more normally hit what was originally the clarinet note. But later on, it was the alto in a singing group. Before... It's only ensembles we're talking about, isn't it?
